notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for **2 Chronicles 28**, drawn from the sources available across the approved sites.

---

## 2 Chronicles 28 — The Evil Reign of Ahaz

---

### v. 1

Ahaz was twenty years old when he became king, and he reigned in Jerusalem sixteen years. And unlike David his father, he did not do what was right in the eyes of the LORD.

- **Ahaz’s reign** (c. 735–715 B.C.) is presented by the Chronicler as the most negative of any king in the book. Unlike other kings who had mixed records, Ahaz’s description is negative from start to finish, beginning with “he did not do what was right” and ending with “provoking to anger the LORD” (v. 25). [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-28-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-28-commentary)
- **The comparison with David** is deliberate: David sinned but repented and sought God’s will. Ahaz chose expediency over obedience. Heritage alone cannot secure righteousness — every generation must choose whom it will serve. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-28-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-28-commentary)
- **“The LORD his God”**: Matthew Poole noted that God was his God “though not by covenant and grace, and special relation, which Ahaz had renounced, yet by his sovereign dominion over him; for God did not forfeit his right by Ahaz’s denying of it.” [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/)
- **Dr. Constable** notes that with Ahaz the Chronicler introduced the prospect of captivity for Judah. Ahaz’s heart was far from God — more like Saul than David — and there is no mention of his ever repenting when God chastened him. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-28.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-28.html)
- **Spurgeon** noted that Ahaz died at about age 36, cut off in the very midst of his sin. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-28-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-28-commentary)
- **The Pulpit Commentary** notes that Isaiah, Hosea, and Micah were contemporaries of Ahaz. His name appears in Assyrian tablets as *Jahukhazi* or Jehoahaz. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html)

*Tradition notes:* Reformed commentators (Olley, Konkel in the ESV Expository Commentary) stress that Ahaz’s reign was a disaster both politically and in covenant faithfulness. Isaiah exhorted Ahaz to “stand firm in your faith” (Isa 7:9b), but Ahaz had already made his own plans. This fits the Reformed emphasis on divine sovereignty and human responsibility — God’s sign of Immanuel was given even to this faithless king. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-28-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-28-commentary)

---

### v. 2

Instead, he walked in the ways of the kings of Israel and even made cast images of the Baals.

- **“He walked in the ways of the kings of Israel”** — this is the first instance in Chronicles where a king of Judah imitates Israel’s apostasy. The northern kingdom had only ungodly kings, and Ahaz followed their pattern rather than David’s. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/)
- **Molten images for the Baals**: Ahaz was not merely tolerating pagan practices; he actively sponsored them. Casting idols for worship was specifically condemned in the Mosaic Law (Ex 34:17). The plural “Baals” suggests a variety of local deities, indicating Judah was being drawn into the full religious system of pagan neighbours. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-28-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-28-commentary)
- **Spurgeon** observed: “God had driven out the Canaanites because of these abominations; therefore, for his own people to practice them, was peculiarly provoking to him. … If we worship the true God under some symbol, the next step is to worship a false God.” [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-28-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-28-commentary)
- **Gill** notes that Ahaz “walked in the ways of the kings of Israel” — meaning the worst of them, like Ahab and Jehoram, who introduced and encouraged the worship of Baal. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/28.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/28.htm)

---

### v. 3

Moreover, Ahaz burned incense in the Valley of Hinnom and sacrificed his sons in the fire, according to the abominations of the nations that the LORD had driven out before the Israelites.

- **The Valley of (the son of) Hinnom** descended eastward below the southern edge of Jerusalem. It became noted as the scene of Judah’s most revolting pagan practices. Later defiled by Josiah and converted into a refuse site, the perpetual fires of “Gehenna” became descriptive of hell itself (Mark 9:43). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/)
- **Child sacrifice**: This describes worship of Molech — a metal statue heated red-hot, onto whose outstretched hands a living infant was placed while drums drowned out the screams. Leviticus 20:1–5 pronounced the death sentence on all who worshipped Molech. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/)
- **Matthew Henry** says Ahaz was “one perfectly divested of all natural affection as well as religion … he burnt his children in the fire to Moloch, not thinking it enough to dedicate them to that infernal fiend by causing them to pass through the fire.” [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-28-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-28-commentary)
- **The Pulpit Commentary** notes this sin of Solomon (1 Kings 11:7–8) is reproduced here — and there can be no doubt this was an incident of the Moloch-superstition. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html)
- The plural “sons” (Chronicles) versus singular “son” (2 Kings 16:3) indicates Ahaz sacrificed more than one child. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-28-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-28-commentary)

---

### v. 4

And he sacrificed and burned incense on the high places, on the hills, and under every green tree.

- Ahaz forsook the temple and worshipped on the hills (“as if they would place him nearer heaven”) and under every green tree (“as if they would signify the protection and influence of heaven by their shade”). [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-28-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-28-commentary)
- **Precept Austin**: The Hebrew verbs *zabach* (sacrificed) and *qāṭar* (burned incense) are terms normally associated with atonement and prayer directed to Yahweh (cf. Ps 141:2). Ahaz took actions meant for the LORD and redirected them to idols. “Religious zeal without revealed truth becomes spiritual adultery.” [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-28-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-28-commentary)
- **Ellicott** notes the chronicler subordinates historical detail to the didactic motive — “not history for its own sake, but history teaching by example.” [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/28.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/28.htm)

---

### v. 5

So the LORD his God delivered Ahaz into the hand of the king of Aram, who attacked him and took many captives to Damascus. Ahaz was also delivered into the hand of the king of Israel, who struck him with great force.

- The conjunction “Therefore” (or “Wherefore”) makes the causal link explicit: Ahaz’s idolatry brought God’s judgment. The king of Aram (Syria) was Rezin; the king of Israel was Pekah. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-28-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-28-commentary)
- **2 Kings 16:5–6** gives the background: Israel and Syria formed an anti-Assyria alliance. Their goal, per Isaiah 7:6, was to dethrone Ahaz and set up a puppet king (“son of Tabel”). [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/)
- **Gill**: “The Lord is called the God of Ahaz, because he was so of right; he had dominion over him, and ought to have been worshipped by him … Ahaz professed he was his God, though in an hypocritical manner.” [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/28.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/28.htm)
- **The Pulpit Commentary**: “The united unsuccessful attacks of Syria and Israel, under Rezin and Pekah respectively, on Jerusalem … are, though so full of interest, all omitted from our chapter.” The Chronicler focuses on the episodes that most illustrate God’s chastisement. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html)

---

### v. 6

For in one day Pekah son of Remaliah killed 120,000 valiant men in Judah. This happened because they had forsaken the LORD, the God of their fathers.

- **The Pulpit Commentary** says the number “is large, but, the uncertainty of very many of these figures notwithstanding, it is impossible absolutely to pronounce it incredible.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html)
- **“Because they had forsaken the LORD”** — this is the Chronicler’s now-frequent refrain. Judgment is always traced to covenant unfaithfulness. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html)
- **Guzik**: The loss of 120,000 soldiers in a single day meant it was a dark time for Judah; it looked as if the Davidic dynasty might soon be extinguished, as so many northern dynasties had been. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/)

---

### v. 7

Zichri, a mighty man of Ephraim, killed Maaseiah the son of the king, Azrikam the governor of the palace, and Elkanah the second to the king.

- **The Pulpit Commentary** notes that “the king’s son” can scarcely mean the child of Ahaz (Ahaz was only about 20 years old). Some think a brother of Ahaz, son of Jotham, may be intended, or it may be a court title for a special official. “The governor of the palace” (or ruler) and “the second to the king” likely refer to high-ranking court officials. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html)
- The loss of these three key officials represented a decapitation of Ahaz’s administration alongside the military disaster. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/)

---

### v. 8

Then the Israelites took 200,000 captives from their kinsmen — women, sons, and daughters. They also carried off a great deal of plunder and brought it to Samaria.

- While the Syrian king carried captives to Damascus, the Israelite king brought his to Samaria. The combined numbers (120,000 slain + 200,000 captives) may be compared with the military strength under Uzziah in 2 Chronicles 26:13. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html)
- The captives were “their kinsmen” — fellow Israelites from the southern kingdom. This makes the crime against brother-tribes especially heinous. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/)

---

### v. 9

But a prophet of the LORD named Oded was there, and he went out to meet the army that returned to Samaria. “Look,” he said to them, “because of His wrath against Judah, the LORD, the God of your fathers, has delivered them into your hand. But you have slaughtered them in a rage that reaches up to heaven.”

- **The contents of vv. 9–15 are not found in the parallel account in 2 Kings**. This is unique to Chronicles and shows the Chronicler’s interest in prophetic intervention. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html)
- **Oded** is not the same prophet who appeared in Asa’s time (2 Chronicles 15:1). We know no other particulars about him. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/28.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/28.htm)
- **“A rage that reaches up to heaven”**: The Pulpit Commentary compares this to Genesis 4:10 (“the voice of thy brother’s blood crieth unto me from the ground”). The rage was so fierce that “upon it the sun ought never to have been required to look.” The figure conveys both magnitude and abominableness before God. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html)
- Oded acknowledged that God had indeed used Israel as an instrument of judgment against Judah, but Israel had exceeded the divine mandate by slaughtering with unrestrained fury. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/)

---

### v. 10

And now you intend to reduce to slavery the men and women of Judah and Jerusalem. But are you not also guilty before the LORD your God?

- The prohibition against enslaving fellow-Israelites is rooted in Leviticus 25:46. The Pulpit Commentary notes: “The moral thread of ordinance that runs everywhere through the divinely established economy of the Old Testament Judaism should be devoutly observed.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html)
- Oded’s argument: Israel was also guilty before God. Their victory was by divine permission, not by their own righteousness. They had no moral standing to enslave their brethren. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/)

---

### v. 11

Now therefore, listen to me and return the captives you took from your kinsmen, for the fierce anger of the LORD is upon you.

- The phrase “fierce anger” points back to the Law and the Prophets — Oded means to say, “You are doing contrary to the Law and the Prophet Moses.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html)
- The command is direct and urgent: release the captives or face divine wrath. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/)

---

### v. 12

Then some of the leaders of the Ephraimites — Azariah son of Jehohanan, Berechiah son of Meshillemoth, Jehizkiah son of Shallum, and Amasa son of Hadlai — stood in opposition to those arriving from the war.

- These four leaders were not part of the returning army; they stood as umpires. The Pulpit Commentary observes: “They were evidently conscious of their past sins, had fear toward God, were not of those who, sinning, hastened to sin yet more; but they wished to flee from the wrath to come.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html)
- Their names and fathers’ names are recorded — a mark of honour in the Chronicler’s style. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/)

---

### v. 13

“You must not bring the captives here,” they said, “for you are proposing to bring guilt upon us from the LORD and to add to our sins and our guilt. For our guilt is great, and fierce anger is upon Israel.”

- The leaders recognized that Israel already had cause for divine displeasure; bringing captives would add sin to sin. The Pulpit Commentary translates: “For to the just cause of offence on the part of Jehovah with us, ye propose to add to our sins.” Their repentant temper was admirable, and they stood in contrast to the callous and reckless majority. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html)
- **Gill** notes they were concerned lest “the fierce wrath of God” already threatened (per Amos and Hosea) should be hastened. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/28.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/28.htm)

---

### v. 14

So the armed men left the captives and the plunder before the leaders and all the assembly.

- The soldiers, remarkably, obeyed. The captives and spoil were surrendered to the leaders and the gathered assembly — a public acknowledgment of wrong. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/)

---

### v. 15

Then the men who were designated by name arose, took charge of the captives, and provided from the plunder clothing for the naked. They clothed them, gave them sandals and food and drink, anointed their wounds, and put all the feeble on donkeys. So they brought them to Jericho, the City of Palms, to their brothers. Then they returned to Samaria.

- **The Pulpit Commentary** calls this “uncommonly graphic in the Hebrew text brevity of description.” The detailed care — clothing the naked, feeding the hungry, anointing wounds, carrying the feeble on donkeys — foreshadows the works of mercy Jesus commends in Matthew 25:34–36. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html)
- **Jericho, the City of Palms**, was well within Judah’s territory, a fertile and shaded spot with plenty of water, from which the captives could easily find their way home. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html)
- **Adam Clarke** commented: “To this beautiful speech nothing can be added by the best comment; it is simple, humane, pious, and overwhelmingly convincing: no wonder it produced the effect mentioned here.” [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/)
- **Guzik** notes the remarkable response: the leaders of Israel recognized their own sin and guilt, cared for the captives from the spoil, and sent them back to Judah. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/)

---

### v. 16

At that time King Ahaz sent for help from the king of Assyria.

- This occurred while the combined armies of Israel and Syria were besieging Jerusalem (2 Kings 16:5). Before Ahaz appealed to Assyria, Isaiah offered him a sign for assurance of God’s help (Isaiah 7:1–12), but Ahaz refused under the pious-sounding excuse of not wanting to test God — when he actually wanted to trust Assyria. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/)
- Ahaz’s message to the Assyrian king was: “I am your servant and your son. Come up and save me” (2 Kings 16:7). He surrendered to one enemy to fight another, refusing to trust the God of Israel. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/)
- **The Pulpit Commentary** notes that “the kings of Assyria” (plural) likely reflects the Hebrew plural for the singular, or a generic reference to Assyrian royalty. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html)

---

### v. 17

The Edomites had again come and attacked Judah and carried away captives.

- The work of Amaziah (2 Chronicles 25:11, 14; 2 Kings 14:7) in subduing Edom was now undone. A weakened Judah invited opportunistic raids from old enemies. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html)
- **Constable**: The Edomites capturing Judahites foreshadows the greater captivity to come. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-28.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-28.html)

---

### v. 18

The Philistines had also raided the cities of the foothills and the Negev of Judah, capturing and occupying Beth-shemesh, Aijalon, and Gederoth, as well as Soco, Timnah, and Gimzo with their villages.

- The Philistines had been subjugated by Uzziah (2 Chronicles 26:6–7); now that work was undone. Each town listed was in the Shephelah (lowlands) or border regions. “They dwelt there” indicates the Philistines obtained a foothold within Judah’s territory. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html)
- **Constable**: “The Philistines took some of Judah’s glory (i.e., towns) captive during the Philistine conquest.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-28.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-28.html)

---

### v. 19

For the LORD humbled Judah because Ahaz king of Israel had thrown off restraint in Judah and had been most unfaithful to the LORD.

- **“Ahaz king of Israel”** — the Chronicler uses “Israel” for Judah here (as in v. 23 and 2 Chronicles 21:2), designating Judah as the true Israel. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-28.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-28.html)
- **“Thrown off restraint”** (or “made Judah naked” / “dealt wantonly”): The Hebrew *hiphrîa‘* means to “let loose” or “cast away restraint.” Ahaz encouraged moral decline. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html)
- **Olley (ESV Expository Commentary)**: While other kings were “unfaithful,” Ahaz was “very unfaithful” and became “yet more faithless.” [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-28-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-28-commentary)

---

### v. 20

Then Tiglath-pileser king of Assyria came to Ahaz but afflicted him rather than strengthening him.

- Tiglath-pileser (also called Tilgath-Pilneser) reigned c. 747–728 B.C. He did strike Damascus and kill Rezin (2 Kings 16:9), providing temporary relief. However, the Chronicler’s deeper moral and religious assessment is that “he bought a master for himself, servitude, tributariness, and the humiliation of disgrace itself.” The temporary relief riveted the yoke of a greater foe around his neck. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html)
- **Guzik**: Ahaz made Judah a subject kingdom to Assyria, sacrificing independence. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/)

---

### v. 21

Although Ahaz had taken a portion from the house of the LORD, from the royal palace, and from the princes and had presented it to the king of Assyria, it did not help him.

- Ahaz stripped the temple, palace, and nobles to pay tribute. The phrase “but he helped him not” shows that Ahaz’s earthly calculations brought no real advantage. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/)
- **The Pulpit Commentary**: “For all Ahaz paid and bribed … he bought a master for himself.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html)
- **Guzik reflects**: “We can only wonder what blessing might have come if Ahaz would have surrendered and sacrificed to the LORD with the same energy and whole heart that he surrendered to the Assyrian king.” [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/)

---

### v. 22

In the time of his distress, King Ahaz became even more unfaithful to the LORD.

- **“This is that King Ahaz”** — a black mark is set against his name. The Pulpit Commentary says the most literal rendering is the most forceful: “He, the King Ahaz.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html)
- **Spurgeon**: “Those who rebel against divine checks, and will not be held in by the providence of God, are to be written down in capital letters as great sinners. They sin with emphasis who sin against the chastising rod.” [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/)
- **Trapp**: “These hammers of the Most High did but beat upon cold iron.” [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/)
- **Constable**: Ahaz hardened his heart even more, like Pharaoh of the Exodus. There is no mention of repentance at any point. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-28.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-28.html)
- **Morgan**: “The evil of his character is supremely demonstrated in that calamities seemed not to have the effect, as they so often had among his predecessors, of rousing him to consciousness of his sin.” [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/)

---

### v. 23

Since Damascus had defeated him, he sacrificed to their gods and said, “Because the gods of the kings of Aram have helped them, I will sacrifice to them that they may help me.” But these gods were the downfall of Ahaz and of all Israel.

- **The Chronicler speaks from Ahaz’s point of view** when saying the gods of Damascus “smote him” — not that the writer believed idols had power, but that Ahaz did. The Syrian gods included Rimmon, Tabrimmon, and Hadad. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html)
- **Gill**: “as it is said of the Indians, that they worship the devil, that he may not hurt them; but that a king of Judah should do this is monstrous stupidity.” [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/28.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/28.htm)
- **2 Kings 16** tells us this happened after Ahaz visited Damascus, where he saw an altar whose pattern he had copied and sent to Urijah the priest — who complied. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/)
- **“All Israel”** — another instance of the Chronicler calling Judah “Israel.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html)
- **Guzik**: Ahaz’s grandfather Uzziah at least falsely worshipped the true God; Ahaz falsely worshipped a false god of his own creation. Uzziah was struck with leprosy, but Ahaz “of a far worse disease, an incurable hardness of heart.” [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/)

---

### v. 24

Then Ahaz gathered up the articles of the house of God, cut them into pieces, shut the doors of the house of the LORD, and set up altars of his own on every street corner in Jerusalem.

- **Cutting the articles in pieces**: Gill says Ahaz “converted them to his own use, sold them, or melted the gold and silver … and made money of them, his treasures being exhausted.” The parallel in 2 Kings 16:17–18 describes his mutilation of the bases, laver, and sea. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/28.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/28.htm)
- **Shutting the doors**: Ellicott notes these are the doors of the sanctuary itself, not the outer court. By closing them, Ahaz suspended all rites performed within the Holy Place and Holy of Holies. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/28.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/2_chronicles/28.htm)
- **Guzik**: “Ahaz could not bring in his pagan, corrupt innovations without also removing what had stood before at the temple. This was an ungodly exchange, taking away the good and putting in the bad.” [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/)
- **Clarke**: “He caused the Divine worship to be totally suspended; and they continued shut till the beginning of the reign of Hezekiah, one of whose first acts was to reopen them.” [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/)
- **Modern Jews** commemorate this crisis by observing a fast. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html)

---

### v. 25

In every city of Judah he built high places to offer incense to other gods, and so he provoked the LORD, the God of his fathers.

- Ahaz systematically established pagan altars throughout the kingdom — “to prevent their coming to Jerusalem to worship,” Gill suggests. What had been a centralized worship of Yahweh was replaced by a decentralized network of idolatry. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/28.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/28.htm)
- **Morgan**: “It would seem as though the light of truth were absolutely extinguished. It was not so, however, for it is likely that throughout the whole reigns of Jotham and Ahaz, Isaiah was uttering his message, and … Micah also was delivering the word of God.” [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/)
- The chapter ends where it began — with the note that Ahaz “provoked to anger the LORD God of his fathers.” The reign was wholly, consistently evil. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-28-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-28-commentary)

---

### vv. 26–27

As for the rest of the acts of Ahaz and all his ways, from beginning to end, they are indeed written in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel. And Ahaz rested with his fathers and was buried in the city of Jerusalem, but he was not placed in the tombs of the kings of Israel. And his son Hezekiah reigned in his place.

- **Burial exclusion**: Ahaz was buried in Jerusalem but denied a place in the royal tombs — a mark of disgrace also given to Jehoram (2 Chronicles 21:20) and Joash (2 Chronicles 24:25). [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-28-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-28-commentary)
- **The Pulpit Commentary** notes the parallel in 2 Kings says he was “buried with his fathers in the city of David,” but not in the sepulchres of the kings — the Chronicler emphasizes the dishonour. [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/2-chronicles-28.html)
- **Trapp**: “He died a natural death, though he was so detestable a miscreant. God putteth off the punishment of many wicked wretches till the other world.” [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/)
- **Hope in Hezekiah**: The mention of Hezekiah’s succession signals a turn. Constable: “Under Ahaz, Judah appeared to have reached its nadir. But for the Chronicler there was always hope of tragedy and despair being turned to rejoicing through repentance.” [https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-28.html](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/2-chronicles-28.html)
- **Guzik** closes: “Ahaz was evil by choice, persistent in evil in spite of calamity, blasphemously rebellious notwithstanding the direct warnings of the prophet of God.” [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/)

## Tradition-Specific Distinctives

### Reformed / Presbyterian

Reformed commentators (John Olley, August Konkel, cited extensively at Precept Austin from the ESV Expository Commentary) emphasise the sovereignty of God displayed in judgment and mercy. The Syro-Ephraite crisis and Isaiah 7 stand in the background — God sovereignly preserved the Davidic line despite Ahaz’s faithlessness. Konkel: “Ahaz could not escape God; the promise of the sign was that God would be with him (Immanuel). God was indeed with him.” The Immanuel prophecy given to a faithless king underscores that the Davidic covenant rests on God’s faithfulness, not human merit. [https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-28-commentary](https://www.preceptaustin.org/2-chronicles-28-commentary)

### Baptist

John Gill (18th-century Baptist) provides detailed verse-by-verse exposition. He notes the horror of Ahaz worshipping the gods of those who defeated him: “that a king of Judah should do this is monstrous stupidity.” Gill emphasises the sufficiency of Scripture and the folly of idolatry. Spurgeon (also Baptist) is quoted stressing that Ahaz “sinned with emphasis” against the chastising rod — a theme of human depravity and the need for sovereign grace. [https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/28.htm](https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/2_chronicles/28.htm); [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/)

### Pentecostal / Charismatic

David Guzik (Enduring Word, Calvary Chapel / charismatic tradition) reads the text with a strong devotional and applicational emphasis. He highlights the spiritual exchange — Ahaz replacing what is good with what is bad — and draws application for believers today. Guzik also emphasises the prophetic voice of Oded as brave and Spirit-empowered, and the miraculous change of heart among the Israelite leaders as a work of God. [https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/2-chronicles-28/)
